definition: Salient means most noticeable or most important — standing out from everything around it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word salient. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know salient should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Forty slides into the safety briefing, only one salient fact followed everyone to the parking lot: the west stairwell floods.
Noticeable is weaker than salient: a noticeable detail catches the eye if you happen to look, while the salient one leaps out and organizes everything else around it.
Glaring is stronger than salient: a salient flaw stands out to a careful reader, but a glaring one is so blatant it cannot be missed — and usually embarrasses someone.

Salient means most noticeable or most important — standing out from everything around it.
The home inspector's report ran nineteen pages, from gutter pitch to attic vents, but its salient finding sat in the first line: the south foundation is sinking.
The buyers forgot the gutters by dinner.
They repeated the foundation sentence to each other for a week, and it alone decided the price.
Salient is the right word because that finding does two things at once: it leaps off the page, and everything else turns on it.
Plenty of details are merely noticeable; the salient one is noticeable because it carries the most weight — the point a reader would be wrong to miss.
formal / analytical — essays, reports, test questions
Salient is the analyst's word: the salient features of a proposal, the salient facts of a case.
Keep it apart from merely relevant — a relevant fact bears on the question but can hide in a footnote, while the salient fact is the one that leaps off the page.
And it is not a synonym for loud: a quiet number can be the most salient thing in a report if everything else depends on it.

New reporters at the city desk all got the same drill from editor Rosa Vane: she would hand over a rambling police report and give them four minutes to find the story.
The reports offered plenty to look at -- times, addresses, witness lists, the makes of cars.
Most trainees fixated on the vivid details.
Vane taught them to hunt instead for the salient one: the fact the whole story would turn on.
In her favorite example, a burglary report mentions, in passing, that the alarm had been switched off from inside.
Everything else on the page is scenery.
Find that fact, she said, and the story writes itself; miss it, and no amount of colorful detail will save you.
